train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 11184/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant asked the Rzeszów District Court to declare that she had been the beneficiary of an inheritance from a certain [Person] on the basis of a will made before a notary on [DATE_TIME]. The court ruled on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Rzeszów District Court asked the Poznań Medical Academy for an expert report to be prepared by the Institute of Psychiatry. It asked if it would accept an expert opinion given by two experts in psychiatry. The opinion was submitted on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant appealed. The appeal was dismissed by the RzesZow Regional Court. It was referred to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court refused to entertain the cassation appeal as no important legal issue arose in the case. The applicant's lawyer lodged a cassation. appeal. The decision was served on the applicant on [ DATE_ TIME].

name: Ali Riza Göktan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 and Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and detained. He consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. As for the couple who had “escaped” arrest by the police, they were in fact both customs officers, known as “Maud” and “[PERSON]”. The applicant completed his prison sentence. However, he remained in custody pursuant to the order requiring him to serve [DATE_TIME] imprisonment in default of payment of the customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out of the Court of Cassation's list. The applicant argued that the order for his imprisonment in default was defective, as the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. The urgent-applications judge dismissed that application in an order of [DATE_TIME]. The Colmar Court of Appeal upheld that order for the following reasons: “Under Article 388 of the Customs Code the court may make an express order for a person who has been convicted of a [customs] offence or offence relating to indirect taxation to remain in custody, even if an ordinary appeal or appeal on points of law has been lodged, until he or she has paid the fiscal penalties imposed on him or her” The applicant was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation and sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and a customs fine. He made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. In dismissing that application, the Court of Appeal found, in particular, that imprisonment in default possesses the legal characteristics not of a penalty, but of a means of enforcement attached to the financial penalties whose recovery they are intended to secure. The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to [LOCATION], where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

name: Eser Ceylan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 14166/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant claims that she had been on her way to her sister's law office when she saw armoured police vehicles firing high pressure water jets and a group of people throwing stones at others in the vicinity. She had to enter the ÖDP (Liberty and Solidarity Party) building in order to protect herself from the police and the demonstrators. After a while, police officers, who had previously obtained a search warrant, entered the building and arrested around fifty persons who were inside at the time, including the applicant. The applicant was charged with taking part in an unauthorised demonstration. The judge of the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance sent a letter to the public prosecutor's office, stating that almost all of the defendants in the case had complained of ill-treatment by the security forces. The public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. He maintained that the complainants had taken part in a demonstration against F-type prisons. Although before intervening and making arrests the police had given the demonstrators a warning and had ordered them to disperse, the demonstrators had resisted the police and thrown stones at them. The Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicant on account of lack of evidence. The Ministry of the Interior lodged an action for compensation against the applicant and the other co-accused. According to the information available in the file, the compensation proceedings were apparently still pending on the date on which the present judgment was adopted. The court's reasoned decision refers to evidence such as eye-witness reports, video recordings of the Security Directorate and other national television channels and other material evidence. In the meantime the Interior requested the reimbursement of the amount of compensation paid to the injured police officers. The application was dismissed by the Kırıkkale Assize Court.

The applicant was accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party) The trial commenced before the Diyarbakır State Security Court and the judge sentenced the applicant pursuant to Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. The judge ruled that the applicant had the right to a lawyer. The Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the applicant was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. The trial is expected to last at least three weeks, if not longer, and is likely to be adjourned until the end of the year.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 20597/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. Her father is an [NRP] national of [N RP] origin. She entered [ LOCATION] on a temporary visa, valid until [Date_TIME]. She was to apply for a residence permit. As proceedings were underway, she was allowed to stay until the decision had become final. The Aliens Police submitted their observations on [DATE_TIME], which were served on the applicant’s counsel. They stated that neither [NRP] Law nor domestic provisions could justify the applicant's sojourn in [LOCATION], which was in fact in breach of section 31 of the Aliens Act. The applicant filed an appeal with the Independent Administrative Panel (IAP) She alleged, inter alia, that the first-instance decision did not comply with EC law. The Administrative Court declined to deal with the case, finding that it did not raise important legal issues. The District Administrative Authority imposed a penal order in the amount of ATS 1,000 with [D date]’ imprisonment in default.

name: Hilmi İzmirli
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 30316/02) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicant complained of a violation of his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. The prosecution accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of the Dev-Yol, whose aim was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a [NRP]-Leninist regime. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Court of Cassation (Yargıtay) acquired jurisdiction over the case. The applicant was released from prison while the appeal was pending. The case was transmitted to the Ankara Assize Court, which held its first hearing on [DATE_TIME]. The Assize court handed down its verdict on the applicant and numerous other accused. The Court ofCassation quashed the verdict, holding that the court should have taken into account some recent legislative amendments affecting the situation of some of the accused. It remitted the case to the assize court, before which the proceedings are still pending. In the meantime, martial law was terminated.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 4789/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8, taken separately or together with Article 14, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was there was no right to a name that was not of the biological mother of the child. The case was decided in favour of the applicant. The court found that the Civil Code, in choosing to regulate only two-parent adoptions, intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as “a biological relationship”. The legal situation obtaining in the present case could not be regarded as unconstitutional. A new regulation entered into force entitled ‘Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”), enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below in a judgment which made no mention of the legislative reform.

name: Srdan Pesukic
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25088/07) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his criminal conviction was based to a decisive extent on testimony given by an anonymous witness. The Government of Montenegro did not express an intention to take part in the proceedings. The case was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant is currently detained in a cantonal prison in [LOCATION] in [ LOCATION]. The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME]. He is represented by Mr [PERSON]. At the beginning of each interrogation, the applicant’s counsel declared that the modalities of the witness interrogations did not allow for an adequate exercise of the rights of the defence. The interrogation was transmitted via a sound link and the witness’ voice was distorted in order to prevent his being identified. The jury court convicted the applicant of manslaughter (vorsätzliche Tötung) and of several counts of drug-trafficking. The court considered that the testimony given by X was credible and pertinent. It noted that X had submitted in a credible and convincing way that his life was in danger in case he testified. The court considered that the measures taken were both necessary and sufficient to prevent identification of the witness. There was no indication that X had been in any way involved in the crime. The court further noted that all persons participating in the decision-making process could gain a personal impression of X. The principle of a public hearing had been safeguarded by allowing the press to follow the hearing from a separate room in which the defence was seated. The jury court considered the information available gave the court a sound basis for assessing the general credibility of the witnesses. It was further known that X spoke the [NRP] language and that he had not been involved in any criminal activity. The jury court resumed its examination by laying out general principles for the assessment of the credibility of evidence by witnesses. It considered that the applicant’s own submissions, according to which he could not have been present at the crime scene as he first entered [NRP] territory in [DATE_TIME] – and thus after the victim had been killed – were contradictory and thus lacked credibility. Conversely, the court considered the testimony given by the anonymous witness, who submitted that he had seen the applicant shooting the victim, to be credible. Relying on all available evidence, the jury court concluded that there was no doubt that [PERSON] had been shot by the applicant. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment and remitted the case to the lower court. The court noted that the anonymous witness had been heard in camera and that the applicant’s counsel did not have the possibility directly to question the witness. Neither the applicant nor his counsel had ever seen the witness, whose personal details remained secret. The fact that the prosecution and the presiding judge were aware of the witness’ identity could not be regarded as a counterbalancing factor as such. Adequate compensation could only be conceivable if at least the defence had the right directly to take part in the interrogation of a witness. However, this possibility was not granted in the instant case. The court examined whether the testimony given by the anonymous witness had to be regarded as being “decisive’ for the applicant’s conviction within the meaning of the “sole or decisive” rule developed by the Court. It noted that the. anonymous witness was the only direct witness of the crime at issue, as the remaining witnesses only gave evidence. by hearsay. The Federal Tribunal confirmed that it had been necessary to protect the witness by shielding his appearance both from the applicant and from the. applicant. It considered that the counsel was not under any legal obligation to transmit information on the witness’ identity to the applicant. The senior public prosecutor lodged a nullity appeal against the decision of the Court of Cassation. The tribunal considered that the testimony given by the witness X had been credible and that it was, furthermore, in line with the scientific conclusion that the victim had been killed by gunshot in the back of his neck on [DATE_TIME]. The tribunal concluded that the anonymous testimony only served as one piece of a mosaic which enforced the conclusion drawn from the remaining evidence. It followed that the criminal courts were not prevented from taking this evidence into account. The tribunal further reviewed the other evidence examined by the jury court and concluded that this evidence, taken separately, would have been sufficient ‘to establish a strong suspicion of a criminal offence, or even to establish his guilt’

It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant is currently detained in a cantonal prison in [ LOCATION] in [LOCATION]. The jury court convicted the applicant of manslaughter (vorsätzliche Tötung) and of several counts of drug-trafficking. The court considered that the testimony given by X was credible and pertinent. It noted that X had submitted in a credible and convincing way that his life was in danger in case he testified, as persons close to the applicant and to [PERSON] were ready to take revenge and did not even hesitate to kill somebody. According to X’s submissions, he was the only person who had observed the crime and who dared to testify. It thus appeared comprehensible that X feared reprisals. The court considered that the measures taken were both necessary and sufficient to prevent identification of the witness. The court took into account that, under the case-law of the European Court of Human Rights, a conviction could not be exclusively based on testimony given by an anonymous witness. There was no indication that X had been in any way involved in the crime. It was further known that X spoke the [NRP] language. All persons participating in the decision-making process could gain a personal impression of X and of his reaction to the questions put to him. The measures taken had been proportionate to the importance of the information available to the court. Jury court resumed its examination by laying out general principles for the assessment of the credibility of evidence by witnesses. The court considered the testimony given by the anonymous witness, who submitted that he had seen the applicant shooting the victim, to be credible. Relying on all available evidence, the jury court concluded that there was no doubt that [PERSON] had been shot by the applicant. The jury court considered that a criminal conviction must not be exclusively based on testimony given to the police by an anonymous witness. It followed that, for formal reasons, these circumstances could not be taken into account and that it had to be assumed in the applicant’s favour that the concrete circumstances had not been proven. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment and remitted the case to the lower court. The court noted that the anonymous witness had been heard in camera and that the applicant’s counsel did not have the possibility directly to question the witness. Neither the applicant nor his counsel had ever seen the witness, whose personal details remained secret. Adequate compensation could only be conceivable if at least the defence had the right directly to take part in the interrogation of the witness and was given the opportunity to assess the witness’ credibility. However, this possibility was not granted in the instant case. The fact that the prosecution and the presiding judge were known to the applicant could not be regarded as a counterbalancing factor as such. According to the case-law of the Court, it was decisive whether the applicant’s defence counsel had been present during the interrogation of the anonymous witness or had at least been in a position to follow the interrogation via an audio‑visual link and to put questions. As this had not been the case, the modalities of the witness’ interrogation did not comply with the standards set up by the Court. The Federal Tribunal quashed the decision of [DATE_TIME] and remitted the case to the Court of Cassation. It considered that the counsel was not under any legal obligation to transmit information on the witness' identity to the applicant. The tribunal concluded that the anonymous testimony only served as one piece of a mosaic which enforced the conclusion drawn from the remaining evidence. It followed that the criminal courts were not prevented from taking this evidence into account. The tribunal reiterated that the jury court had considered that the testimony given by the witness X had been credible and that it was, furthermore, in line with the scientific conclusion that the victim had been killed by gunshot in the back of his neck on [DATE_TIME]. The Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s nullity appeal. On [Date_TIME] the Federal Tribunal rejected the applicants’ appeal.

name: Marcus Orr
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 31283/04) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the convention on account of the national court’s decision, despite his acquittal on criminal charges, to order him to pay compensation to the victim. On an appeal by the applicant, the Eidsivating High Court held a fresh hearing in the case. The jury answered the questions relating to the charges in the negative (no reasons are given by a jury). The professional judges decided to pass judgment on the basis of the jury's verdict and acquitted the applicant by a judgment of [DATE_TIME]. The High Court, consisting of the professional judges, considered the claim [DATE_TIME]. By two votes to one the High Court concluded, in the same judgment, that the applicant was liable and ordered him to pay NOK 74,000 in compensation for pecuniary damage and NOK 25,000 for non-pecuniarydamage. The court bases the judgment on the jury’s verdict. [The applicant] is therefore acquitted of the indictment raised against him. Despite the fact that [the applicant] has been acquitted of having, with intent or gross negligence, raped [[PERSON], under [NRP] law, she has not thereby lost her possibility to claim compensation. The High Court unanimously finds that on the balance of probabilities it is clearly probable that [the applicant] during [DATE_TIME] had sexual intercourse with [Ms C.] The applicant called her at her hotel room with the pretext that he needed to borrow or to get some drinks as he himself had ‘gone dry’. He went to the mini-bar and fetched something to drink, but instead of leaving he sat down on her bed and started talking. After a short time he began pulling her quilt in order to remove it. She asked him to leave, but he did not follow her suggestion. [The applicant] continued to pull the quilt and drew her towards himself and also got himself undressed. In the end they were both in the bed. The applicant’s appeal within the company against his dismissal from his job as a pilot for British Airways was refused. He appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's procedure, assessment of evidence and application of the law. The Appeals Selection Committee granted leave to appeal with respect to this ground of appeal, while refusing such leave for the remainder. The appeal on the latter point was on the ground that, contrary to Article 6 § 2 of the Convention, the. High Court had failed in its judgment to make it sufficiently clear that the order to pay compensation did not affect his acquittal of the charges. The majority found that on the balance of probabilities it was clearly probable that [the applicant] understood that [[PERSON] did not want sexual relations with him, but nonetheless forced coitus upon her. There was a requirement under the European Court’s case law relating to Article 6 § 2 of the Convention that the reasoning stated in the judgement be worded in such a way as not to cast doubt on the correctness of the acquittal. In this case, the High Court had failed to create the necessary distance between the two issues, since the reasoning in the judgment went on immediately thereafter to deal with the subject of compensation. This came so close to establishing that the conditions for criminal sexual assault had been fulfilled that the presumption of innocence must be deemed to have been violated. If there was no basis for setting the impugned judgment aside, then at the very least a declaratory judgment ought to be rendered. The High Court ruled that the reasons given by the High Court do not contravene the presumption of innocence in Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The evidentiary requirements in civil actions are less stringent than those that apply in criminal cases. The possibility to review the claim for compensation in the criminal case has clear advantages from the point of view of procedural economy and saves the victim from the financial and emotional burden of undergoing two trials. An appeal against the decision will not succeed, according to the European Court of Justice (ECC) in the case of [PERSON] [no. 34964/97, ECHR 2003‑II]. The ECHR ruled that a person acquitted of a criminal charge can be ordered to pay compensation in a civil case. A person who has been acquitted of a criminal charge may be ordered to pay compensation in the same case. The ground for the appeal is that the reasons given in the High Court’s judgment on this point violated the presumption of innocence. It is a condition in both of these provisions that the tortfeasor has inflicted on the victim a violation of the type provided for in Article 192 of the Criminal Code. The court must therefore make it clear that it has found proven a fact which from an objective point of view constitutes a breach of this provision. This must be avoided, in view of the strict evidentiary requirements that apply in criminal cases. train_texts: The case was lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 74976/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Secretary of State for Trade and Industry issued proceedings against the applicant and four others under section 6 of the Company Directors Disqualification Act (“the CDDA”) The Secretary of State’s evidence was completed and served on the applicant on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant applied to strike out the proceedings. The applicants and three other defendants were acquitted and two defendants were convicted. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed. The appeal to the High Court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr [PERSON], could proceed and was heard and dismissed. The strike-out and disqualification proceedings resumed and were adjourned generally, with liberty to restore. The Secretary of. State decided that it remained expedient in the public interest to continue. The application to quash the convictions was dismissed. Mr [PERSON] was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal. His substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on [DATE_TIME]. The court found that the reasons for the Secretary of State’s failure to complete his evidence before the proceedings were commenced had been ‘far from satisfactory’ But it considered nonetheless that the case should proceed since it was in the public interest to determine the ‘particularly serious’ allegations of false accounting and trading while insolvent made against the defendants. The Registrar ordered that if the defendants had not served their evidence by [Dates] they would be debarred from adducing any evidence. The applicant asked the Secretary of State to reconsider the continuance of the disqualification proceedings against him. On [DATE_TIME] the Secretary Of State informed the applicant that he intended to continue. The applicant was willing to negotiate a “Carecraft’ settlement. The time-limit for the applicant’s further evidence was extended indefinitely. The matter was set down for trial on [DAT_TIME]. The applicant applied for judicial review of the legality of the decision of [DETAIL_TIME], not to discontinue the proceedings. The application was denied and the trial was adjourned until next week. The applicant agreed that he would sign the “Carecraft” statement if he failed in the judicial review proceedings. The disqualification proceedings were adjourned. The application for leave to apply for judicial review was refused. The applicant appealed to the House of Lords, which granted leave on [DATE_TIME]. The House heard the applicant’s appeal and delivered judgment dismissing it on the grounds that the House had no jurisdiction to hear an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal refusing leave. The Secretary of State wrote to the applicant indicating that he wished to fix a hearing at which the ‘CareCraft’ order could be made. Vice-Chancellor held most of the time elapsed is to be attributed to the requirements of justice down to the conclusion of the criminal proceedings in [DATE_TIME] or to the conduct of Mr [PERSON]. Such conduct includes the attempt to strike out the proceedings concluded in. [Date_TIME], the negotiations for a summary disposal under the Carecraft procedure from [DATED_TIME), and the renewed attempts for that purpose. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, which also refused leave to appeal. The Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them, the Vice- chancellor said. The applicant responded with three further applications. The Secretary of State applied to have these proceedings struck out, on the grounds that they raised identical issues to the application dismissed by the Vice-Chancellor. The applicant signed an undertaking which provided for an agreed period of disqualification of [DATE_TIME]. The undertaking was accepted and the proceedings against the applicant were terminated. On appeal, the two convictions were quashed in the High Court. The strike-out and disqualification proceedings resumed and were adjourned generally. The applicant and one other defendant were acquitted, and two defendants were convicted. The appeal to the High court brought by the first defendant to the disqualification proceeding, Mr [PERSON], could proceed and was heard. Mr [PERSON] was granted leave to appeal out of time to the Court of Appeal, and his substantive appeal was dismissed by that court on [DATE_TIME]. The court found that the reasons for the Secretary of State’s failure to complete his evidence before the proceedings were commenced had been “far from satisfactory” But it considered nonetheless that the case should proceed since it was in the public interest to determine the “particularly serious” allegations of false accounting and trading while insolvent made against the defendants. The court observed that the delay by the secretary of state had not affected the timing of the hearing or prejudiced the applicant, and that, once the proceedings had commenced, the respondents’ main concern was to delay the proceedings until after the conclusion of the criminal trial. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant asked the Secretary of State to reconsider the continuance of the disqualification proceedings against him. Vice-Chancellor held: “Most of the time elapsed is to be attributed either to the requirements of justice down to the conclusion of the criminal proceedings in [DATE_TIME] or to the conduct of Mr [PERSON’s]” The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal, which also refused leave. The applicant renewed his application at an oral hearing on [Date_TIME], at which the Court. of Appeal again refused leave to appeal, on the basis that there had been no violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Secretary of State now to proceed with these proceedings would not be incompatible with them. The Secretary of State applied to have these proceedings struck out, on the grounds that they raised identical issues to the application dismissed by the Vice-Chancellor. The applicant responded with three further applications. Patten J struck out the applicant’s new action and dismissed his further three applications. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant signed an undertaking which provided for an agreed period of disqualification. The undertaking was accepted and the proceedings against the applicant were terminated. The application was later dismissed. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47117/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the criminal proceedings. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). Law Court convicted the applicant of membership of an illegal organisation and sentenced him to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. Military Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the Diyarbakır Martial Law Court on the ground that the latter had misinterpreted the domestic law in respect of the offence in question. Law no. 3953 abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Courts. The applicant was released from detention and is now free to go back to his old job as a plumber in Turkey. He is not allowed to contact his former employer, who is the head of a private firm in Ankara. He has been released from prison and is free to return to his former job.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30) The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of [LOCATION] of a provincial highway, the L 52. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to [DATE_TIME], but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices. The Court heard addresses by them and also their replies to its questions. The authorities consulted several experts. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file. The Zumtobel partnership thereupon applied to the Constitutional Court. It claimed that the expropriation proceedings had violated its right of access to a court with full jurisdiction, guaranteed inter alia by Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The Office considered the first request to be irrelevant to the case; as to the second, it stated that the official expert had not shown any bias in favour of the authorities and had submitted a convincing report. On [DATE_TIME] the Office made an order for expropriated and fixed compensation at 620 schillings per square metre. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on [DATE_TIME], after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing (see paragraph 20 below) In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the decision. The fact that the Government Office had not made the commencement of construction work for the L 52 subject to a decision was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. Final decision on the length of the route was not incompatible with the Provincial Highways Law. Environmental protection was taken into account when assessing the various relevant interests. The fact that an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the [DATE_TIME] Law to doubt his complete impartiality. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt for the purposes of Article 7 (1), sub-paragraph 4, of the law. The applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it could not claim a right of access to that file. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention. The court declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court to determine the amount of compensation. On appeal the amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50 [NRP] schillings (ATS). train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his continuing preventive detention violated his right to liberty as provided in Article 5 § 1 of the convention. He was convicted of numerous offences, which, apart from one conviction for assault, were directed against the property of others. These included fraud, theft and aggravated theft, handling of stolen goods and extortion. The Cologne Regional Court convicted the applicant on seven counts of joint aggravated robbery. It sentenced him to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and ordered his preventive detention. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Regional Court found that the applicant had robbed seven banks together with one or two accomplices. In each case, he and his accomplice(s) had threatened the bank employees with loaded guns and collected between 4,450 and more than half a million German marks (DEM) The applicant had twice been sentenced to terms of imprisonment of [DATE_TIME] (for several acts of fraud, embezzlement, theft and burglary). He had a disposition to commit serious offences and was therefore dangerous to the public. He had caused substantial material damage and had acted with considerable criminal energy. He did not feel like working and financed his very costly lifestyle through crime. The applicant had repeatedly served long prison sentences. Despite the fact that he had kept committing increasingly serious offences for. [DATE_TIME] in order to obtain substantial amounts of money. As confirmed by the convincing report of a psychiatric and neurological expert, [PERSON]., it was to be expected that the applicant would commit further offences against the property of others if released. The applicant had been convicted on two further counts of fraud causing damage amounting to DEM 200,000, committed during the period of supervision of his conduct. He had been sentenced to both imprisonment and preventive detention. He has served the sentence imposed in the judgment of the Hagen Regional Court and has been in preventive detention since. The Aachen Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s request for the suspension on probation of his preventive detention as ordered by the Cologne Regional Court. The Regional Court found that there was no basis to expect that the applicant, if released, would not commit further serious offences. It further declared that no request for review of this decision would be admissible within a [DATE_TIME] period (Article 67e § 3 of the Criminal Code – see paragraph 49 below) The proceedings at issue were heard before the Aacen Regional Court in September 2014. The applicant is still liable to commit offences causing considerable economic damage, as demonstrated by his past acts of fraud, which had caused considerable damage. The Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of [DATE_TIME]. He claimed that in view of his poor state of health, he could no longer be considered dangerous and complained that he had not had the conditions of his detention relaxed in any way. The court found that his preventive detention was still necessary because there was still a risk of his committing serious offences causing considerable damage to property. The applicant was convicted of two counts of fraud and sentenced to a total of 20 years in prison. He was also sentenced to 12 years of probation. The sentence was suspended for a period of three years after he was released. The applicant’s failure to reflect on his offences had been confirmed by the governor of [LOCATION]. The latter had considered that the applicant's personality, which was the cause for his committing offences, had not changed. As he had no family or friends outside prison, he could, if anything, be placed in a supervised residence. But it could not be ascertained whether he was sufficiently ready to cooperate. The public interest in the detention of the applicant, who still risked committing serious property offences, continued to prevail over his own interest in personal liberty. The Court of Appeal noted that the negative prognosis as to the applicant‘s future conduct could partly have been caused by misconduct on the part of prison management. Should the prison authorities persist in refusing such measures, it was for the applicant to seek their enforcement before the courts, the court said. The applicant was not so poor as to render his detention disproportionate. The Court of Appeal ruled that there was no risk that the applicant would commit serious offences resulting in considerable psychological or physical harm to the victims. The courts had repeatedly considered that he might commit only non-violent property offences if released. The applicant was released, accordingly, on [DATE_TIME] and has been living in a residential care home in Erkelenz since then. He has regularly been granted leave under escort. He is currently in a care home with no contact with the outside world. He was sentenced to two years in prison for aggravated robbery and one year for attempted robbery. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 62543/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by five [NRP] nationals. The applicants complained that they had not had a fair hearing in the judicial proceedings brought by them to halt construction of the Itoiz dam. They also complained that the Autonomous Community law in question had been enacted with a view to preventing execution of a Supreme Court judgment which had become final. In their opinion, the enactment of that law had interfered with their right to a fair trial as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1. The case originated in an engineering project of [DATE_TIME] for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the procedure for informing the Audiencia Nacional. The Chamber declared the application admissible and reserved its position on the Government's preliminary questions as to whether the first five applicants lacked ‘victim’ status and had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that, according to the law, the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan, which had not been drawn up when the project was approved. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam and for a breakdown of the quarry use that would be necessary for its construction. All the parties to the proceedings lodged súplica appeals against the decision of [DATE_TIME]. In the context of the interim enforcement of its judgment of [ DATE_ TIME] and, in particular, with a view to maintaining the protection zone around the three nature reservesaffected by the project, the Audiencias prohibited the filling of the reservoir and displacement of the population. The Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves. The size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of [PERSON], where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. Counsel for the State and the government of the Autonomous Community of Navarre had appealed on points of law against the Audiencia Nacional's judgment of [DATE_TIME]. The central State authorities and the Navarre Autonomous community's government argued that it had become legally impossible to enforce the Supreme Court's judgment. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of [DATE_TIME] was inapplicable in the instant case. The Audiencia Nacional asked the Constitutional Court to rule on the preliminary question submitted by the applicant association. Under section 37(2) of the Judicature Act, it gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies. The Constitutional Court declared the issues raised in the Preliminary Question admissible and extended the question to include section 18(3) (A.1.) and (B) of that law. The applicant association submitted its observations on [Date_TIME]. The Constitutional Court held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of [DATE_TIME] were compatible with the Constitution. The Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies indicated that the Chamber would present no observations. The Audiencia Nacional forwarded to the Constitutional Court the written pleadings submitted by the applicant association during the proceedings before it. The government and parliament of [PERSON] and the [NRP] government, and invited them to file their observations, submitted their observations on 11 and 15 November. The Constitutional Court's judgment was handed down on 15 November 2013. It held that enforcement of the Supreme Court's. judgment of [ DATE_ TIME], delivered in accordance with Navarre Autonomous. Community Law no. [Date_TIME], had become impossible since the entry into force of. the new law. The Constitutional Court ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, it was justifiable that the explanatory memorandum accompanying the Autonomous Community law of [DATE_TIME] specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three above-mentioned nature reserves. The Constitutional Court found that both the Supreme Court's judgment and the new Autonomous community law were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around theThree nature reserves affected by the project's construction. The court found that the system of peripheral Protection zones introduced by this new law had not in itself been considered arbitrary in the Audiencia Nacional's decision. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. It held that the balance of general interests had been respected. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on [DATE_TIME]. held responsible for the serious deterioration of the environment. The application had claimed that the new legal rules governing the peripheral protection zones around the nature reserves appeared in a law rather than in regulations, as had previously been the case. The Constitutional Court noted that there was no legal provision requiring that certain subjects be dealt with by regulations. The Government submitted their observations on [DATE_TIME], after an extension of the time allowed, and the applicant replied. The Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations. The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], and the decision was made in favor of the Government. The application was examined by the President of the Court, Mr J.-P. Costa, the judge elected in respect of [ LOCATION] and the other members. The applicant’s mother died on [DATE_TIME] of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, [PERSON], born out of wedlock and legitimised by his mother's marriage. On his birth certificate only his mother’S name was entered as a parent. She was still married at the time of his birth, but living separately from her husband. The applicant, as an adulterine child, could not lay claim to more than a quarter of the estate. He requested the court to hold that he had the same inheritance rights as a legitimate child. The applicant appealed, arguing that Article 760 of the Civil Code was incompatible with Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The Nîmes Court of Appeal upheld the provisions of the lower court’s judgment ordering the estate to be divided and determining the applicant's inheritance rights. It considered, however, that the amount transferred to the applicant’‘s account should be returned to the estate because he had not proved that his mother had intended it as a gift.’ The court concluded that Article760 was necessary in order to protect the rights of others and that it was a principle of public policy which was not contrary to the Convention. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation, which delivered its judgment on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant’s complaint of unjustified discrimination on grounds of birth between children born in [LOCATION] and children born out of wedlock, contrary to Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention, was dismissed. The court was also properly entitled to hold that Article 760 of the Civil Code was a provision necessary for the protection of the rights of others, that it was a [NRP] legal principle of public policy and that it wasn’t contrary to the European Convention on Human Rights.” “The. provision does not intentionally discriminate against adulterine children, but ensures the. protection of children born of the marriage who might be disadvantaged on the. division of their parents’ estate by the presence of an adulterous child”

The case originated in an application (no. 34406/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The Commission decided to give notice of the application to the French Government (‘the Government’) and to invite them to submit observations in writing on its admissibility and merits. The Government submitted their observations on [DATE_TIME], after an extension of the time allowed, and the applicant replied. The Court declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations at a hearing. The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION]. The applicant’s mother died on [DATE_TIME] of HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) encephalopathy. She left two children: a son, [PERSON], born out of wedlock and legitimised by his mother's marriage. The applicant, as an adulterine child, could not lay claim to more than a quarter of it. The Court heard addresses by Mr [Person] and Mrs Dubrocard. the Montpellier Bar, Counsel. the applicant also attended the hearing. The hearing continued until the end of the hearing on 11 November 2014. The jury returned a verdict in favour of the applicant. The court conceded that Article 760 of the Civil Code represented a derogation from the principle that children should be treated equally regardless of descent. But it held that its purpose was not to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth but to ensure minimum compliance with marital commitments on the part of the married parent who engenders an illegitimate child. The Court of Appeal concluded that Article760 was necessary in order to protect the rights of others and that it was a principle of public policy which was not contrary to the Convention. It considered, however, that the amount transferred to the applicant’s account should be returned to the estate to be divided because he had not proved that his mother had intended it as a gift. The court was properly entitled to hold that it was not the intention of the legislature to discriminate between children on the grounds of their birth. The Court of Cassation held that in deciding that the facts of the case had not shown any intention on the part of the deceased to bestow a gift on her son, the Court of Appeal had determined an issue which it alone had jurisdiction to determine. The Commission of the Compensation Fund for Transfusion Patients and Haemophiliacs awarded the applicant, in his personal capacity, compensation of 40,000 French francs (FRF) and assessed the deceased’s loss at FRF 500,000, to be paid to her heirs.
